Microsoft Copilot & Power Platform · Preview Capability Guide

Managed Apps (Preview)

Apps built in Copilot Cowork, Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, or an SDK-compatible tool, published onto Microsoft Copilot Managed Runtime in your tenant, and governed from the Microsoft 365 admin center. How to build them, how they version toward production, how to govern them, and how the usage-based bill actually works. · Updated September 2026.

The one thing to remember: a managed app is real full-stack code deployed to Microsoft Copilot Managed Runtime, an enterprise platform inside the Microsoft 365 tenant boundary. The app can originate in Copilot Cowork, Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, or an SDK-compatible tool; once deployed, it inherits Microsoft Entra identity, governed data access, lifecycle controls, and centralized oversight in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Commercially it is a hybrid, and that is the part people get wrong: building and running are metered as two separate services in Copilot Credits, but a user holding Power Apps Premium has their license checked first, so runtime is included within that license's allowance of 40,000 Power Platform requests per user per 24 hours. AI-powered runtime inside the app always consumes credits on top.

1. What a managed app actually is

App building starts as a conversation. A user chooses App (Preview) from the Copilot Studio home screen, or invokes the /app skill in a Copilot Cowork chat, and describes the business outcome, the users, the data, and the actions they need. Agentic coding turns that intent into a working app scaffold. From there the user iterates in natural language, previews the app, and can inspect the underlying code when they want more control.

What comes out the other side is deliberately not a toy:

The artifact

A full-stack app built on open standards

  • Real code, inspectable and extensible by developers who want to go deeper.
  • Git-backed source control, deployment stages, and version isolation, so the next version can be improved without disturbing the live one.
  • Published apps are discovered by users at managedapps.cloud.microsoft.com, or opened from a share link.
The platform around it

Enterprise controls, on by default

  • Microsoft Entra authentication and authorization with no extra identity configuration.
  • Access to more than 1,500 connectors, plus Work IQ for organizational context.
  • Conditional Access, DLP, advanced connector policies, sharing limits, and data source restrictions applied automatically.
  • Microsoft-managed environments that inherit those policies rather than requiring you to configure them.

Build where you want, run on one managed foundation

The important structural fact is the separation between open creation and managed operation. Cowork and Copilot Studio remain the natural-language entry points most information workers and makers will see, while Copilot Code and the Copilot Managed Runtime SDK extend the same model to professional developers and compatible third-party tools. The build experience can change without changing the operating model: deployed apps use the same runtime, identity, governed data access, Git-backed lifecycle, security policies, inventory, and monitoring.

Apps, agents, and workflows are three different tools

Copilot Studio now hosts all three, and the reason to care is that people reach for the wrong one constantly. They are not competing options; they solve different shapes of problem, and a serious business process often needs more than one.

Structure

Apps

Guide a person through data, forms, lists, and actions in an interactive experience. Reach for an app when a human needs a place to go and work.

Reasoning

Agents

Answer questions and take action conversationally. Reach for an agent when the problem is interpretation and judgment rather than structured data entry.

Consistency

Workflows

Execute repeatable steps against defined triggers with defined outcomes. Reach for a workflow when the process must happen the same way every time, without a person.

In combination

Most real processes

An intake app, a workflow that routes and notifies, and an agent that answers questions about the backlog. Building all three in one studio is the actual argument for this capability.

Name collision worth getting straight before a customer conversation. "Managed apps" is the Microsoft 365 admin center's term for apps built this way. It does not mean Managed Environments, and it is not the same thing as a Power Apps code app or a Power Apps vibe app, even though all three involve generated code. The admin center draws the line explicitly, and the line is about where the app is governed.

2. Building one

1

Describe the outcome, not the screens

State the business problem, who uses it, what data it needs, and what actions it takes. You can reference Microsoft 365 sources directly — documents, spreadsheets, meetings, messages. "Build an app to run my daily scrum with my team" is a legitimate starting prompt; so is a paragraph describing an onboarding tracker with its data sources named.

Specificity about data and actions pays off more than specificity about layout. Layout is cheap to change in the next turn. A missing data source means the scaffold is built around the wrong shape.

In Copilot Studio you can also choose the model and the reasoning level before generating. Treat that as a real lever: a higher reasoning level on a genuinely complex first generation usually costs less than three corrective turns afterward.

2

Let it connect the data

Apps use connectors to reach business data, and Work IQ to reach organizational context inside the Microsoft 365 tenant boundary. This is not read-only: an app can surface information, take action, and write results back to the connected system. The app-building skill can also generate a data schema in supported connectors and hand you an app with those sources already wired.

1,500+ connectors Work IQ organizational context Schema generation Read and write
3

Iterate in conversation, inspect the code when you need to

Ask for changes in natural language — add a feature, change a layout, modify how data is displayed — and each change is applied and reflected in the preview without manually rebuilding the interface. Information workers can stay entirely in the conversation.

Advanced makers and developers can switch between the live app and a code view, or show both at once, to inspect the files created during generation. That matters for two reasons beyond curiosity: it is how a developer validates that the generated app does what it claims, and it is the path to extending the app when a scenario needs deeper control. An app nobody can read is not an enterprise asset.

One caveat worth setting expectations on: the in-product code view is read-only today. Makers inspect the generated files and request changes through conversation. Direct code editing is available through the developer toolchain covered in section 8, not from inside the building experience. If someone demonstrates this capability and says "and you can just edit the code right here," that is the part to check against the current build.

4

Work from the app workspace once you have more than one

In Copilot Studio, Apps in the navigation opens a workspace listing the apps you have built. Search by name and review publishing status, owner, environment, and last modified date; open one to keep building, or use Play to test it as a user would. This becomes the maker's home surface quickly — the tile on the landing page is for starting, the workspace is for operating.

5

Publish, then share deliberately

Publishing makes the app and your latest changes available to the people you share it with. Sharing works like a Word document or a PowerPoint deck: generate a link and send it to anyone in your organization who can use Microsoft 365 Copilot, or add users directly.

Tell every builder this once, in these words: anyone with the share link can open and use the app including all of its data. A share link is a data-access decision, not a convenience. Share only with the people who should see what the app can see.

The inverse also catches people out: sharing an app does not necessarily share its underlying data. Because apps reach data on behalf of the signed-in user, a recipient may still need their own permissions or their own connection to the source before the app works for them. Confirm that app users have the permissions and connections the data sources require, rather than assuming the share covers it.

What makers can do today, and what they cannot yet

Supported

In the building experience

  • Create an app from a natural-language description.
  • Generate screens, forms, fields, tables, views, filters, actions, and sample data.
  • Preview and interact with the app while it is being built.
  • Request changes to layout, data, or behavior through conversation.
  • Use supported files, lists, tables, and data connections available in the environment.
  • Inspect generated files in a read-only code view.
  • Publish the latest version and share with permitted people or groups.
Current limitations

Worth saying out loud before a pilot

  • Complex apps with many roles, conditional paths, integrations, or specialized rules may require more iteration.
  • Code view is read-only; changes are requested through conversation.
  • Sharing an app may not share its underlying data; users may need separate permissions.
  • Results may vary across languages and cultural contexts.
  • Preview features, limits, connections, and deployment options may change before general availability.
  • Safety instructions and content filtering are in place, but AI-generated results can still be inaccurate or unexpected. Review and test every app before making it available to others.

Maker practices that actually change the outcome

  • Clearly describe the app's purpose, intended users, data, fields, actions, and business rules.
  • Break complex requirements into smaller changes and review after each one. A long list of changes in a single turn is how makers lose track of what broke.
  • Test with representative accounts and data before using production data or sharing broadly.
  • Confirm that app users have the permissions and connections needed for the data sources.
  • Use the personal developer environment for creation, iteration, and testing, subject to tenant and environment policies.
  • Test the main scenarios, calculations, links, accessibility, permissions, connections, and error handling before publishing.
  • Publish only when the main scenarios work, and share only with people who should be able to use the app.

What a good first prompt looks like

The difference between a usable first generation and a frustrating one is almost entirely in how much structure the prompt carries. Compare a bare request with one that names the fields, the roles, the states, the views, and the notifications:

Create an app to manage equipment maintenance requests.

Include an intake form capturing: asset ID, fault category, priority,
reported-by, description, requested completion date, and photo attachments.

Assign each request to an owner, a reviewer, and an approver.

Use the statuses: New, Triaged, In progress, Blocked, Completed.

Add views for My requests, Awaiting my approval, and All open requests.

Notify the owner when a request is assigned and the requester when
the status changes.

Everything in that prompt is a decision the generator would otherwise make for you, and every one of those decisions is cheaper to state than to correct. Layout is the one thing worth leaving vague — it is trivial to adjust in the next turn.

3. Versioning and the path to production

This is the section that separates a managed app from a disposable prototype, and it is the part most easily missed in a demo.

Apps follow familiar application lifecycle management principles. The app's human-readable source can be versioned through Git-backed source control. Makers can preview and test changes before publishing. Crucially, there is version isolation: the published version stays stable in production while the next version is being built, so iteration does not put the live experience at risk.

Why this changes the conversation: the standard objection to AI-generated apps is "fine for a prototype, unsafe for anything real." Separate build, preview, and publish stages with a stable production version answer that directly. It is the difference between a clever demo and something you can put a business process on. When you evaluate this capability, evaluate this, not the speed of the first generation.
These apps are not solution-aware, and that is a deliberate architectural break. Apps built in Copilot Studio use a net-new app model that is not tied to Power Platform solutions. Application metadata and the ALM model use source control and standard source-control-based ALM instead. If your organization's deployment discipline is built around solutions, managed layers, and the Power Platform admin center, this capability does not slot into it. That is not a defect, but it is a conversation to have with whoever owns your ALM standards before the first app matters to anyone.

The Microsoft-operated runtime

A published app runs on Microsoft Copilot Managed Runtime, a Microsoft-operated platform inside the Microsoft 365 tenant boundary. The host runs both the client and service logic and applies organizational security and policy to it, rather than handing you an artifact you then have to host and secure yourself. Microsoft introduced the host and SDK in public preview in September 2026; the platform already powers apps built through Copilot Cowork, Copilot Code, and Copilot Studio. What that runtime supplies:

  • Microsoft Entra identity for authentication and access control.
  • Conditional Access enforcement.
  • Advanced connector policies and data loss prevention.
  • Monitoring and inventory, so administrators can see what exists.
  • Usage analytics out of the box, without instrumenting the app yourself.

The practical consequence: there is no hosting decision, no certificate to manage, no identity integration to write, and no separate monitoring stack to stand up. That is most of the reason this is worth using instead of generating a web app with a coding agent and hosting it yourself.

Shared responsibility

The cleanest way to answer a security reviewer asking "who is on the hook for what?" is to draw the line once and keep drawing it in the same place. You control the app. Microsoft operates the identity, policy, and runtime layer beneath it.

What you ownWhat Microsoft operates
The app: its screens, logic, and contentThe Microsoft-hosted runtime the app runs on
The app's code, built on open web standards, which you can inspect and take ownership ofMicrosoft Entra sign-in
Which data sources and connectors the app uses, within your organization's policiesEnforcement of connector policies and tenant boundaries at runtime
Whether the app can be shared, and when a new version is publishedInventory, monitoring, and usage reporting in the Microsoft 365 admin center
Deciding who is accountable for each published appPlatform security for the hosted runtime

Published apps use Microsoft-hosted infrastructure and approved application dependencies. Customers do not provision infrastructure, configure hosting, or stand up a deployment pipeline for these apps.

Work IQ: organizational context, not just data access

Apps integrate natively with Work IQ, which contributes three distinct things worth separating:

CapabilityWhat it means in the app
ContextThe app understands the user and the organization around them — people, relationships, and how work connects.
DataRetrieval of work and business data that is permission-aware, so a user sees only what they are already entitled to see.
WorkspacesSecure retention of user inputs and app outputs, so the app has somewhere to keep state.

Permission-aware retrieval is the detail to raise with a security reviewer. It means the app does not become a way to see data the user could not otherwise reach.

What these apps connect to, and what they do not require

More than 1,500 prebuilt connectors, plus native connections to Dataverse, Dynamics 365, Microsoft 365, Fabric, and Azure. Work IQ and Fabric IQ ground the app in organizational context such as calendars, documents, processes, and structured data, which is the substantive difference from tools that start with mock data and leave integration until later. Which sources and operations are actually available depends on the environment and your organizational policies.

Dataverse is not required, and there is no default data store. The maker explicitly selects the data source. Apps can use connectors and API-accessible sources including SharePoint, Dataverse, SQL, PostgreSQL, and anything else exposing an API. Dataverse can be chosen as the app's data store when the scenario calls for it, but an app does not need Dataverse simply because it is enterprise-grade. Unlike traditional Power Platform applications, these apps do not rely on Dataverse for application metadata, solutions, or ALM — that layer moved to source control. Pick the data source on its data, security, and integration merits, not out of habit.

Composability: MCP, workflows, and agents

Two facts that matter more than they first appear:

  • Apps and their skills can be exposed as MCP servers, which lets Copilot and agents invoke them as callable skills. That is the foundation for composability and for in-conversation app experiences, and it means an app is not only a destination a person visits.
  • An app can call a workflow or an agent to complete an end-to-end scenario, which is the practical argument for building all three in one place.

Both are worth noting on the cost side as well: MCP tool calls and agent invocations are AI-powered runtime, and AI-powered runtime is metered regardless of license position. See section 6.

4. What sits underneath

Managed apps run in Microsoft-managed environments, and enabling app creation changes Power Platform environment routing in your tenant whether or not you were using it before. This is the part administrators find out about late, so it is worth reading carefully.

  • Environment routing is turned on automatically for apps, in every tenant, and cannot be changed. It is a premium governance feature and apps enable it by default.
  • Makers are routed to their own personal developer environments, which are managed environments by default. In a tenant with no prior routing rules, a rule routing Everyone to personal developer environments is created automatically, along with a new default environment group.
  • Tenants with existing routing rules do not get that new rule, which means some makers may be unable to use apps until an admin adds a rule covering Everyone. If you already use routing, this is an action item, not a notification.
  • The Everyone rule must sit last in priority order, and only one rule may target Everyone. Existing configurations that violate either constraint must be cleaned up before any further routing changes can be made.
  • These personal developer environments have no Dataverse initially. Dataverse is added automatically only when the maker visits a Power Apps or Power Automate maker surface and lands in that environment, or an admin adds it deliberately.
  • Tenants with no Power Platform deployment at all still get a baseline. Where an organization has not configured policies, or has never deployed Power Platform, a default environment group is created with a baseline set of policies already in place. App-specific policies for sharing and content security are applied by default and can be adjusted afterwards from the Microsoft 365 admin center and the Power Platform admin center.
Environment policy is the real boundary. What an app is permitted to do is decided by the environment it was created in, not by the app. Connector permissions and data access policies scoped to that environment constrain what the app can reach both while it is being built and after it is published. If you want a different answer for a group of makers, change their environment, not their app.
The licensing tripwire hidden in that list: a maker who only builds managed apps in their personal developer environment does not need a Power Apps or Power Automate premium license, and auto-claim does not apply. The moment that maker creates a Power Apps or Power Automate resource in that environment, they do need the appropriate premium license to satisfy managed environment requirements, and auto-claim does apply. The boundary is the resource type, not the environment.

5. Governing them

Governance follows the app from build through publish and run. Existing policies are inherited from the maker's Power Platform environment, and enforcement stays with the app at runtime rather than being applied once at deployment. Apps access connected data on behalf of the signed-in user, so publishing or sharing an app never grants access to data a person could not otherwise reach.

Control areaWhat applies to an appWhere it comes from
IdentityMicrosoft Entra sign-in and per-app Conditional AccessYour existing tenant identity configuration
DataConnector permissions, data policies, and advanced connector policiesThe policies scoped to the app's environment
Audit supportGit-backed change history, inventory and activity signalsThe app lifecycle and the admin center inventory

Choosing where people can build apps

App creation is available to makers by default, and apps can be created in more than one place. Wherever they are made, the same rules apply to them. Administrators choose which creation paths are open to the organization from Microsoft 365 admin center → Apps → Overview, under Choose where people can make apps:

  • Copilot Studio — makers build apps in Copilot Studio. On by default, and the recommended path.
  • Copilot Cowork — people create apps through chat. Availability is governed by your organization's participation in the Frontier program.

Turning a path off prevents makers from creating new apps that way. Apps that are already published continue to run. Beyond the on/off switch, administrators can restrict which makers are able to build apps in Copilot Studio via API or PowerShell, so a defined group can evaluate the capability before it is opened more widely. That is the control to reach for in a staged rollout: a pilot cohort rather than a tenant-wide flip.

Enablement

  1. Copilot Cowork access is granted by a spending policy, not by an allow list. Cowork is generally available, and the old practice of allowing or blocking users on the Cowork agent entry under Agents → All Agents no longer controls access. Access exists when a spending policy includes the user and selects Cowork as a service.
  2. Enabling or disabling Cowork enables or disables app building by default. They are not separate switches.
  3. App creation in Cowork additionally requires Frontier enrollment, which only a Global Administrator can complete. Power Platform administrators cannot enable it and are directed to contact someone who can. AI Administrator, AI Reader, and Global Reader are view-only for this.
A spending policy is an access control, not just a budget. Any user in scope of a policy that selects Cowork can use Cowork, regardless of how small the limit is. A policy with a one-credit limit still grants access. To keep someone out, leave them out of every Cowork-selecting policy rather than setting their limit low. Administrators who try to fence off access with tiny limits end up with access they did not intend to grant and a support queue they did not expect.

The inventory: Microsoft 365 admin center → Apps → All apps

Every published app appears here automatically, with no manual registration. Created, updated, and deleted apps show up within about 15 minutes.

WhereWhat you get

Two actions that matter

Reversible

Block

Immediately stops end-user access while preserving the app and its data. Users attempting to launch it see a blocked status. Use this for an app under investigation — flagged for non-compliance, suspicious behavior, or a security concern — where deletion would destroy evidence. Unblock once resolved.

Permanent

Delete

Permanently removes the app, with a confirmation dialog summarizing the effect. This is the housekeeping tool for abandoned, test, and duplicate apps — which, in a tenant where anyone can produce an app in a conversation, is a category that grows on its own.

Who can do what

RoleApp inventory
Global AdministratorFull: view, delete, block
Power Platform AdministratorFull: view, delete, block
AI AdministratorRead-only
AI ReaderRead-only
Global ReaderRead-only

Compliance work the inventory is genuinely good at: spotting apps running in non-approved regions, spotting apps outside expected environment groups, and identifying owners without chasing people across tools.

Visibility and lifecycle, paired

Each app in the inventory carries the context needed to decide whether it needs attention, and the action to act on that decision. Read the two columns together; visibility without a corresponding action is just a report.

What you can seeWhat you can do

Decide who is accountable for overseeing published apps before makers begin publishing, as you would for any other application estate. This is the cheapest governance decision available and the one most often deferred until the inventory is already crowded.

6. Licensing and cost

There are two meters here, and they are funded differently. Building and running apps are metered as two separate services under usage-based billing, paid in Copilot Credits, from the same pool and governance model as Cowork itself. But a user's Power Apps Premium license is checked first at runtime, so where Premium is already deployed, much of the run cost is already covered. Getting this wrong in either direction produces a badly wrong forecast, so separate the two before you model anything.

Two meters, metered separately on purpose

Building and running apps are both charged through Copilot Credits usage-based billing, but they are metered as two separate services. That separation is deliberate, and it is useful: it lets you manage cost for app makers and for app users independently.

  • Building an app consumes credits during authoring. Consumption varies with the language model used, the complexity of the app, and the amount of generation and iteration involved. This is the maker-side cost, and it rises with the number of makers and how much they iterate.
  • Hosting, running, and managing an app consumes credits once the app is deployed to the Microsoft-managed host. Consumption varies with the volume and complexity of the tasks the app processes. This is the user-side cost, and it scales with adoption.
What drives consumptionHow it is charged
Connector API callsCopilot Credits
Mid-tier API calls
Active users
Number of apps
AI tools

The Power Apps Premium entitlement, precisely

Microsoft's request-limits documentation states it plainly: the capability to run apps built in Cowork is included with Power Apps Premium. The current app-management guidance generalizes the same rule to apps built in Copilot Studio: when someone runs an app, their Power Apps Premium license is checked first. If they hold one, usage is included within existing Power Apps Premium request limits. If they do not hold one, or once the request limit is reached, usage is billed through Copilot Credits usage-based billing.

DetailWhat it means
The allowance 40,000 Power Platform requests per user per 24 hours — the standard Power Apps Premium limit, not a separate app-specific pool. It is a daily figure, which is roughly 1.2 million a month, so it is far more generous than a monthly reading of the same number would suggest.
What counts Power Platform requests generated as the app runs. Named explicitly: data connector calls, app launches, asset loads, and build and publish actions.
Licenses that do not include it Power Apps per app, Power Apps pay-as-you-go, and Dynamics 365 licenses that include Power Apps capabilities. This is the trap: holding a Power Apps license of some kind is not sufficient. It must be Premium.
Never included AI-powered runtime — agents and Work IQ APIs invoked by the app — sits outside these limits and consumes Copilot Credits regardless of which license the user holds.
Stacking A user with multiple paid licenses gets the sum of their allowances. Someone holding both a Dynamics 365 Enterprise base license and a Power Apps per user license has 80,000 requests per 24 hours.
Two ways people misread this. First, as "40,000 operations a month" — it is per user per day, roughly thirty times larger, and reading it as monthly makes the entitlement look far tighter than it is. Second, as "Power Apps Premium covers apps built this way, so there is no credit cost" — it covers running them, not building them, and it never covers AI runtime inside the app. Note also that the entitlement is Premium only: it is not included with Power Apps per app, Power Apps pay-as-you-go, or Dynamics 365 licenses that carry Power Apps capabilities.

Planning for cost

The precise entitlement sentence, worth memorizing: Power Apps Premium does not cover building — building is charged through Copilot Credits. Power Apps Premium covers non-AI runtime within the existing 40,000 daily API-call limit per user. Usage above that limit, and AI-related calls such as Work IQ, agent invocations, and MCP tools, are charged through usage-based billing. Three clauses, and most misquotes drop one of them.

A worked example, because the percentages mislead

Take 100 users, 50 of whom hold Power Apps Premium, all using the app equally. The intuitive answer is "half the cost is covered." The accurate answer is more useful:

  • The 50 Premium users are partially covered. Their non-AI runtime is included, subject to Power Apps Premium request limits.
  • Copilot Credits apply to the 50 users without qualifying coverage, to AI-powered runtime for all 100, and to any covered user who exceeds the request limits.
  • The share of licensed users is not sufficient to calculate consumption, because consumption depends materially on what the app does. A Premium user on an app with no AI-powered runtime may consume no credits at all, while AI-powered runtime consumes credits for everyone regardless of license.
Credit estimates are not a per-user-per-app rate. Published examples are estimates that already account for app complexity, how much the app is used, and how many people use it. They are not a fixed monthly figure you can multiply by a headcount. Adding apps, adding users, or adding more sophisticated functionality each move the number independently.

Look at your existing Power Apps Premium footprint first. If the people who will use these apps already hold Premium, a substantial share of runtime consumption may already be covered, and your exposure is concentrated in authoring and in AI-powered runtime rather than in everyday use. If they do not, runtime is billed from the first request and should be modeled accordingly.

  • Separate the two cost curves when you forecast. Authoring cost rises with the number of makers and how much they iterate. Runtime cost rises with how many people use the resulting apps and how hard those apps work. A pilot with five makers and fifty users has a very different shape from one with fifty makers and five hundred users, even at similar total spend.
  • Plan for AI-powered runtime separately. Because agents and Work IQ APIs sit outside request limits, an app that calls them frequently behaves differently from one that mostly reads and writes business data. That difference will not show up in a licensing conversation that only considers user counts.
  • Get real numbers rather than estimates. A pilot focused on one team and one process over a defined period produces actual consumption data, which is a far more reliable basis for budgeting than anything modeled before the app is running.

Credit caps, and what is coming

Cost management for these apps is handled from the Microsoft 365 admin center. Credit caps apply per user today, for both maker and runtime consumption, and are managed through Copilot Credits usage-based billing.

  • For makers, a cap is a per-user app-building budget. It can be standardized across the organization or tailored to groups such as departments with their own budgets, which is what limits authoring cost as makers iterate.
  • For end users, caps currently work the same way, applying per user to runtime consumption.
  • Environment-level controls are expected within the next few months. For end-user runtime consumption they are the more natural long-term fit: an environment-level cap behaves like a project budget, covering everyone working on a given project rather than each person individually. If per-user caps feel like an awkward instrument for your runtime scenario, that is because they are, and it is a gap with a stated fix.

What sits inside usage-based billing

The Microsoft 365 admin center currently manages these services under usage-based billing:

  • Cowork itself — model responses, tool and skill calls, image generation, browser tasks.
  • Apps built with Copilot Cowork — the building, and the running where it is not covered by a Power Apps Premium entitlement.
  • Work IQ API — including when an app calls it.

More services are added over time, and spending policies have Auto-apply new services enabled by default. If you want new services reviewed before they inherit an existing policy, turn that setting off deliberately. Otherwise a future service quietly joins a budget someone already approved.

How you pay

MechanismWhat it isWhere it is configured
Prepaid Copilot CreditsCapacity packs purchased up front and drawn down.Copilot → Cost management → Configuration
Pay-as-you-goBilled against a connected Azure subscription as consumed.Copilot → Cost management → Configuration
Spending policiesScope which users and groups may consume, which services are covered, organization-level and user-level limits, alerts, and the billing method.Copilot → Cost management
Credit requestsUsers request access or a higher limit; administrators route and approve.Copilot → Cost management → Credit requests

The Cost management dashboard reports consumption by policy, user, group, agent, and service. Reader roles can review consumption without gaining permission to change policies or billing configuration, which means finance and licensing stakeholders can be given visibility without being given control. Use that separation rather than handing out administrator roles for reporting.

Preview behavior to warn users about: a user who does not meet the credit requirements to run an app first receives a warning. Access is then blocked after 20 app operations or five minutes of use, whichever comes first. If a pilot audience has not been placed in a funded spending policy, they will hit that wall mid-demo and conclude the app is broken.

The cost mistakes worth pre-empting

  • Assuming there is no per-user option. There is. Where users already hold Power Apps Premium, the run cost for Cowork-built apps is already covered, and the remaining variable is the build activity and any AI runtime. An organization with a large Premium estate is in a very different position from one starting cold.
  • Assuming a Power Apps license is a Power Apps license. Per app, pay-as-you-go, and Dynamics 365 licenses carrying Power Apps capabilities do not include this. Check the actual SKU before promising anything.
  • Reading the allowance as monthly. 40,000 requests per user per 24 hours. Getting this wrong understates the headroom by roughly thirty times and leads to buying capacity nobody needs.
  • Forgetting AI runtime is always metered. An app that calls an agent or the Work IQ APIs consumes Copilot Credits on every invocation, whatever license the user holds. An app that calls an agent on every page load is a consumption decision disguised as a design decision.
  • Using low limits as an access control. Covered above, and worth repeating because it is the single most common misconfiguration: inclusion in a Cowork-selecting policy is the grant.
  • Leaving auto-apply on without deciding to. It is on by default and it is the right setting for many organizations. It should still be a decision someone made.
  • Missing the premium-license boundary in personal developer environments. Building managed apps there does not require Power Apps or Power Automate premium. Creating Power Apps or Power Automate resources in that same environment does, with auto-claim in play.
  • Ignoring what sits behind the connectors. Neither credits nor a Power Apps license pays for the third-party SaaS, Azure services, or Dynamics 365 licensing that the connectors reach into.
  • Pricing a preview. Frontier previews run under existing preview terms, and capabilities and availability may change. Confirm against the Copilot Credits Guide and the Power Platform Licensing Guide before putting a figure in a proposal.

7. Power Apps, Copilot Studio, or Cowork?

This is the question that comes up in every conversation about managed apps, and the binary framing is the wrong one. Both are enterprise-ready. They differ in authoring experience and commercial model, not in whether they can be trusted with a business process. The right question is which one fits the problem in front of you today, on the understanding that you can combine them later.

It is really a three-way choice, and the cleanest way to make it is to start with what the customer is building and how they want to build it rather than with the products:

ChooseWhen
Power AppsStructured requirements, detailed design control, predictable economics, and traditional low-code development. Also the default where there are existing Power Apps or Dynamics investments, or sustained high-volume usage.
Copilot StudioA dedicated environment for creating and refining applications through natural-language conversation — for business-process owners and contributors who also build workflows and agents, or who spend significant time building.
Copilot CoworkApp creation through conversation inside the Microsoft 365 Copilot experience, in the flow of work — for information workers already using Copilot daily who want to spin up something for themselves or their team.

These are not mutually exclusive. Different makers and different scenarios within the same organization will land in different places, and that is the expected outcome rather than a governance failure. Copilot Studio and Cowork are two entry points into the same managed-app model, so the choice between those two is about where the person wants to work, not about what they get.

Predictable and precise

Power Apps fits when…

  • The organization already owns and runs Power Apps, with the skills and governance in place.
  • Costs must be fully predictable and forecastable per user, not variable with usage.
  • The workload is tied to Dynamics 365 or deep Dataverse data modeling.
  • Design precision matters — drag-and-drop layout control and Power Fx for exact logic.
  • Governance is expected to live in the Power Platform admin center.
  • The app itself is the deliverable, with AI optional rather than central.
Fast and consumption-based

Copilot Studio fits when…

  • You want to widen who can build beyond the existing maker community.
  • The organization prefers usage-based billing and wants to start without licensing every potential user up front.
  • Microsoft 365 Copilot is already deployed and Copilot Credits are already being managed.
  • The process needs an app, an agent, and a workflow together.
  • Natural-language authoring with optional code inspection suits the people doing the building.
  • Governance is expected to live in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
The commercial distinction, restated: these are not two sealed pricing worlds. Power Apps is per-user licensing — higher certainty, paid whether or not the app is used heavily. Copilot Studio app building is consumption — no new SKU to get started and no need to license a potential audience in advance, but a bill that moves with usage. They overlap: Power Apps Premium already includes the capability to run apps built in Cowork, within its 40,000 requests per user per 24 hours. So an organization with an established Premium estate can adopt this with the run cost largely covered, leaving build activity and AI runtime as the variable. Which approach is cheaper depends on the licenses already in place and how concentrated the usage turns out to be — and the second of those is usually unknown until after the app exists.

Three things that are true regardless of which you start with:

  • Existing Power Apps investments carry forward. Apps keep running. Business logic, Dataverse tables, and connectors to systems of record keep doing their job and can be reused across apps, workflows, and agents. Choosing Copilot Studio for a new build does not strand anything already built.
  • An existing Premium estate is an asset here, not a sunk cost. It already carries the entitlement to run Cowork-built apps. Check what is deployed before assuming a greenfield consumption model.
  • The choice is a starting point, not a boundary. Start with whichever experience and commercial model fits, then combine apps, agents, and workflows as the requirement develops. Treating it as a permanent architectural fork creates a decision that does not need making.

What does not change

The continuity story is more reassuring than most people assume, and it is worth stating plainly because the absence of a statement gets read as a threat:

  • Nothing is being announced that changes Power Automate, Power Pages, or Dataverse. Existing Power Platform capabilities continue as they are, and existing investments — Dataverse tables, connectors, policies, business logic — remain part of the broader application strategy.
  • Canvas and model-driven apps continue unchanged. There is no migration path and no requirement to move. Customers should keep maintaining and extending those applications on their own merits.
  • Power Apps code apps remain supported as a capability of Managed Environments, and remain licensed through the existing Power Apps licensing model. Rebuilding a code app as a managed app may introduce credit-based consumption, and the two architectures have real capability differences, so confirm requirements and feature parity before moving anything. This is not a promoted migration motion.
  • If you are evaluating Power Apps right now, do not pause. Power Apps remains the right choice for structured business applications that need detailed maker control, design precision, and predictable licensing. The new experiences add a natural-language creation path; they do not put the existing one on notice.

8. The developer path

Managed apps are real code, and the Copilot Managed Runtime SDK is the connective layer between that code and the host. It gives Microsoft tools, compatible third-party tools, and professional developers a common path from local development to an enterprise-managed runtime. It is worth knowing this exists, because it is the answer to "what happens when our developers want to own this properly?"

  • @microsoft/managed-apps-cli on the public npm registry, providing the ms binary: create, dev, add data sources, build, pack, deploy, play, share, and delete. Companion packages supply the SDK and a Vite plugin.
  • Typed connector services for TypeScript. Developers define the app's data connections and generate typed services for governed access to connectors, enterprise data, identity, and Copilot work context.
  • One lifecycle toolchain. The CLI and SDK cover scaffolding, project configuration, local preview, deployment, and versioning rather than appearing only at the packaging step.
  • Bring-your-own-tool support. SDK-compatible third-party development experiences can deploy to the same host. Microsoft cites Lovable as an example: the app can keep its familiar build experience while gaining tenant sign-in, policy enforcement, and centralized inventory when it runs.
  • First-party project templates and a coding-agent plugin that works with GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code, published in the microsoft/Managed-Apps repository.
  • GitHub Actions for CI/CD: install the CLI on the runner, pack the app, and deploy it as a service principal with no developer in the loop.
  • Least-privilege connector policies. When a connection reference is shared, the app must declare in its config which connector operations it is permitted to invoke, and the Connectors infrastructure enforces that limit per app. Tabular references declare per-table verbs; action connectors declare action IDs. Declaring everything satisfies validation and protects nothing, so infer the set from what the code actually calls.
This is a preview toolchain. The repository states plainly that APIs, templates, and tooling may change before general availability. Treat pinned versions and a rollback plan as mandatory rather than prudent.

9. When to reach for this, and when not to

SituationBetter answer
A team needs an interactive tool over Microsoft 365 and business data, and needs it this weekManaged app. This is exactly the scenario, and the governance comes with it rather than after it.
A business process needs an app, an agent, and a workflow working togetherCopilot Studio, building all three side by side.
An individual or small team wants to remove a recurring manual taskManaged app from Cowork, shared by link to a named few.
Standard forms over Dataverse with business process flows and records managementModel-driven app. You would be rebuilding a great deal of supplied behavior.
Costs must be forecastable to the penny before the project startsPower Apps. Per-user licensing trades flexibility for certainty, which is the correct trade in some organizations.
Pixel-level design control, or logic complex enough to want an expression languagePower Apps, with drag-and-drop layout and Power Fx.
A developer team wants to own a web app in their own repository with their own pipelinePower Apps code apps, or the managed apps CLI path above. Note that code apps are governed in the Power Platform admin center, not the Microsoft 365 admin center.
An external, anonymous, or unauthenticated audiencePower Pages. Managed apps authenticate every user with Entra ID and share to people who can use Microsoft 365 Copilot.
A conversational interface that reasons over knowledgeA Copilot Studio agent. An app is a structured experience; an agent is a conversation. Build both when the process needs both.
A regulated, tier-one production workload going live this quarterWait, or use a generally available option. This is preview, under preview terms, with capabilities that may change.

10. Rollout checklist

Before you turn it on

  • Confirm Frontier enrollment is possible and identify the Global Administrator who will do it.
  • Decide which creation paths stay open under Apps → Overview → Choose where people can make apps, and whether to restrict Copilot Studio app building to a pilot group via API or PowerShell before opening it more widely.
  • Name the person accountable for overseeing published apps before makers start publishing.
  • Set credit caps for makers, and for end users if they will not be covered by Power Apps Premium. Caps are per user today; environment-level controls are expected later.
  • Set up usage-based billing: choose prepaid, pay-as-you-go, or both, and connect the Azure subscription if required.
  • Author the spending policy as an access decision first and a budget second. Scope it to a security group you control.
  • Audit which users already hold Power Apps Premium before modeling cost. That entitlement covers running apps built in Cowork; per app, pay-as-you-go, and Dynamics 365 licenses with Power Apps capabilities do not.
  • Decide consciously whether Auto-apply new services stays on.
  • Check your existing Power Platform environment routing configuration before enabling apps. If you already have routing rules, plan the rule covering Everyone and verify the priority order, or some makers will not be able to use apps.
  • Give finance and licensing stakeholders reader access to the cost dashboard rather than administrator roles.

In the first month

  • Watch the All apps inventory weekly while the initial wave is created. This is when ownership and duplication are cheapest to fix.
  • Set alert rules on the Monitor tab for the apps that matter, rather than waiting for users to report problems.
  • Review the Data & tools tab on any app that reaches more than a handful of users, and confirm the connectors match what you expected.
  • Check that anything heading for real production use is actually being versioned, with the published version left stable while the next one is built. An app being edited live in production is a prototype wearing a production badge.
  • Filter for apps in non-approved regions or outside expected environment groups, and act on what you find.
  • Brief builders that a share link exposes the app and its data to anyone who receives it.

Ongoing

  • Keep a deletion rhythm for abandoned, test, and duplicate apps. Prototype volume only ever grows.
  • Use Block rather than Delete for anything under investigation.
  • Export the inventory periodically for offline review and reporting.
  • Re-read the preview terms at each notable capability change. In preview, the contract moves.
